title: Early Civilizations: Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus, China and the Americas
length_note: 13 classes, each 30 to 40 minutes. Mesopotamia comes first, as Mike asked, and gets three classes. It is the longest-studied case and sets up the questions we ask of every other place: writing, cities, law, religion, trade and everyday life. Egypt gets three classes because its evidence is rich and its writing, religion and state need room. The Indus, China and the Americas each get two classes. The Indus and the Americas have fewer decoded texts, so the evidence is different. The last class compares them all and places them on one timeline. Each class is built from three or four short parts, so learners can take breaks, including adults relearning after a brain injury. Every class ends with a short 'what else was happening in the world' segment. No class is padding, and each of the six topics (writing, cities, law, religion, trade, everyday life) is covered for every region.

classes.title: Mesopotamia I: Rivers, Farms and the First Cities
classes.goal: Explain in plain words what 'civilization' means, say why farming between the Tigris and Euphrates led to cities, and name early Sumerian cities on a map.
topics: What historians mean by 'civilization' and why the word is debated
How we know: archaeology, tablets, mounds (tells)
Geography: the Tigris, Euphrates, floods and irrigation
From villages to cities: Uruk and other Sumerian city-states
Temples, rulers and how a city was organised
Outside Mesopotamia at the same time: early farming villages elsewhere

classes.title: Mesopotamia II: Writing, Law and Religion
classes.goal: Describe how cuneiform began and what it was used for, give an example of Mesopotamian law, and explain how religion shaped city life.
topics: Cuneiform: from accounting tokens and tablets to literature
Scribes and schools
Early law codes, including Ur-Nammu and Hammurabi, and what they show about society
Gods, temples and priests
Myths and stories such as Gilgamesh
Outside Mesopotamia at the same time

classes.title: Mesopotamia III: Trade, Everyday Life and Empires
classes.goal: Describe a typical day for different kinds of people, say what Mesopotamians traded and with whom, and outline how city-states became empires.
topics: Food, houses, family, work and women's roles
Craft, markets and long-distance trade
Akkad, Babylon and Assyria in outline
Mathematics, the calendar and technology
Outside Mesopotamia at the same time

classes.title: Egypt I: The Nile, Unification and the Pharaoh
classes.goal: Explain how the Nile shaped Egyptian life, and describe how Egypt became one kingdom and how its cities and government worked.
topics: The Nile, the annual flood and farming
Upper and Lower Egypt and unification
Kingdoms in outline: Old, Middle and New
The pharaoh as ruler and as a sacred figure
Cities, towns and administration
Comparison with Mesopotamia: a river, but a different kind of state

classes.title: Egypt II: Hieroglyphs, Religion and Law
classes.goal: Describe Egyptian writing and its uses, explain beliefs about gods and the afterlife, and say how justice and order (ma'at) worked.
topics: Hieroglyphs, hieratic, papyrus and scribes
The Rosetta Stone and how hieroglyphs were deciphered
Gods, temples and priests
Burial, mummification and the afterlife
Pyramids and tombs: who built them and why
Law, courts and ma'at

classes.title: Egypt III: Trade, Everyday Life and Neighbours
classes.goal: Describe daily life for farmers, craftworkers and elites, name Egypt's main trading partners and goods, and say what was happening elsewhere at the time.
topics: Farming, food, housing, clothing and family life
Craft, labour and taxes
Trade by river and sea, including Nubia and the Levant
Contact with Mesopotamia
Outside Egypt at the same time: the Indus and early China

classes.title: The Indus Valley I: Planned Cities and Water
classes.goal: Describe what Indus cities such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa were like and what their layout tells us.
topics: Geography: the Indus and neighbouring river systems
How the civilization was found and excavated
City planning, drains, wells and standard bricks
Weights, measures and crafts
Compared with Mesopotamia and Egypt: few obvious palaces or royal tombs

classes.title: The Indus Valley II: Script, Beliefs, Trade and Change
classes.goal: Explain why the Indus script is still undeciphered, say what we can and can't know about religion, law and rulers, and outline the main ideas about the civilization's decline.
topics: The Indus script and seals: what we know and don't
Possible religious practices, and the limits of the evidence
Trade with Mesopotamia and other regions
Everyday life: food, clothes, ornaments, toys
Debated causes of decline: climate and river changes
Outside the Indus at the same time

classes.title: Early China I: The Yellow River, Early Farming and the Shang
classes.goal: Describe how early communities grew along China's great rivers, and explain what oracle bones tell us about Shang writing, kingship and belief.
topics: Geography: the Yellow and Yangtze rivers
Early farming cultures: millet and rice
Erlitou and Shang cities
Oracle bones and early Chinese writing
Ancestor worship and divination
Bronze casting and its uses

classes.title: Early China II: Zhou Rule, Ritual, Trade and Daily Life
classes.goal: Explain the idea of the Mandate of Heaven, describe how rule, ritual and law worked in early China, and describe everyday life and trade.
topics: The Zhou and the Mandate of Heaven
Ritual, social order and early ideas about law
Farming, crafts, silk and village life
Trade and contact with neighbours
Outside China at the same time

classes.title: The Americas I: Caral, the Olmec and Early Cities
classes.goal: Explain that civilizations arose independently in the Americas, and describe early sites in the Andes and Mesoamerica.
topics: Why the Americas matter: independent origins
Crops: maize, potatoes, squash and beans
Norte Chico and Caral in Peru
The Olmec: San Lorenzo, La Venta and the colossal heads
Religion, ritual architecture and ball games
Trade networks and everyday life

classes.title: The Americas II: Maya Writing, Calendars and the Andes
classes.goal: Describe Maya writing and calendars, outline how Maya city-states were governed, and describe Andean ways of recording and organising without alphabetic writing.
topics: Early Mesoamerican writing and the Maya script
Maya calendars and astronomy
City-states, kings, law and warfare
Religion and sacrifice
The Andes: Chavín, textiles and khipu (knotted cords)
Trade and everyday life
Outside the Americas at the same time

classes.title: Putting It All Together: Compare, Connect and Place on One Timeline
classes.goal: Compare how writing, cities, law, religion, trade and daily life developed in all five regions, and place them on one shared timeline with what else was happening.
topics: One timeline for all regions
Side-by-side comparison table of the six themes
What they share and where they differ
Contact and independent invention
Why some civilizations declined or changed
Limits of the evidence: what we still don't know
Review and self-check
